scenes.visual: WDollar — the ep11 particle $1, frozen mid-form, one particle drifting
scenes.text: Eighty days ago I made you a promise. Wire the money end to end, in the open, and let you watch the first real dollar land — or fail to. No staging. No tricks. Counter at zero, on camera.

scenes.visual: particles hold; the bottom-bar counter fades in reading $0.00
scenes.text: That counter is live. It reads zero. By the end of this episode it either reads one dollar — or it still reads zero, and you'll know exactly why.

scenes.visual: beat — red accent, single particle drops into a slot
scenes.text: Let's build the coin slot.

scenes.visual: WStakes — stakes card over dark room; no title repeat
scenes.text: Nine products. Eight workers. Fifteen thousand dollars a year going out. And in eleven episodes, not one dollar coming in. Tonight that changes — or it doesn't, and you see the failure, frame by frame.

scenes.visual: WFourBoxes — four empty boxes draw in: CHECKOUT · WEBHOOK · LEDGER · PAYOUT
scenes.text: First, a definition. Most 'we take payments' demos stop at box one: a checkout page. That's a doorbell, not a door. Wired end to end means four things, in order. A checkout a stranger can pay. A webhook that proves the payment really happened. A ledger that writes it down once — and only once. And a payout that puts the money in a bank account with a human name on it.

scenes.visual: the four boxes dim; the top-right PIPE panel appears with a pointer sign
scenes.text: That panel in the corner is the pipe. Four segments. Dark means unproven. Each one lights only when you have seen it work. Watch it.

scenes.visual: WRepo — SiteFrame: github.com/DansiDanutz/purchase-webhook (private; blur nothing sensitive, show the README)
scenes.text: Here's the part nobody expected. The pipe was already written. Back in July the fleet built this — purchase-webhook. Stripe sends a signed event, the service checks it, and on a real paid order it grants the buyer access to a private repository. Code as the product. Payment as the key.

scenes.visual: WAudit — SiteFrame: the July audit report; rows land one by one; stamp-hit on each
scenes.text: And it was audited. Twenty-seventh of July. Five high-severity findings — all fixed. Seven medium and low — all fixed. Zero critical open. A signed event alone no longer proves a purchase; it has to match the mode, the product, the amount, and the currency the server owns.

scenes.visual: WNotClaimed — the audit's own line in red: "Production is deliberately not claimed"
scenes.text: And then the honest line, written by the auditor: production is deliberately not claimed. Because the ledger lives in a small database with a file lock — it needs a machine that remembers. Not a serverless function that forgets between requests. So for eighty days the pipe sat on the shelf. Finished. Unplugged.

scenes.visual: WDeploy — terminal plate, real: the deploy to the stateful host, health check returns ready
scenes.text: So tonight we plug it in. Step one: a home. One container, one worker, one lock — exactly what the audit demanded. ❓HOST NAME. Readiness comes back green only when the database and the configuration are both present. It does.

scenes.visual: WKeys — terminal plate: environment variables set; every value redacted on screen
scenes.text: Step two: the keys. Live mode, not test mode. The secret key, the webhook signing secret, the product mapping the server owns. You will not see a single value on this screen. Not blurred. Never rendered.

scenes.visual: WEndpoint — SiteFrame: Stripe dashboard, webhook endpoint registered; glitch-zap if the first attempt fails
scenes.text: Step three: Stripe has to know where to knock. One endpoint. One event type. Stripe sends a signed test ping — the service checks the signature and answers two hundred. The first segment lights. CHECKOUT. The second lights. WEBHOOK.

scenes.visual: WLedger — terminal plate: a test-mode event lands; ledger row written; replay the same event; row count stays 1
scenes.text: Step four, the one that matters. Send the same event twice. A bad ledger writes it twice and gives the product away twice. This one writes it once. Replay — one row. Replay — one row. LEDGER lights.

scenes.visual: WNervixPay — SiteFrame: nervixpay.live live; chapter open, whoosh
scenes.text: Now a confession. While Stripe sat on the shelf, the company grew a second coin slot — and it's been live for weeks. NervixPay. Crypto payments for any website and any service. No processor. No approval. The money goes wallet to wallet, straight to the merchant.

scenes.visual: WTwoPipes — two pipes side by side: FIAT · CRYPTO; the flywheel mini-map from ep11 in the corner
scenes.text: Two pipes, two kinds of customer. Fiat for people with a card and a company name. Crypto for the builders already living on-chain. The flywheel from last episode doesn't care which coin turns it. It only cares that one does.

scenes.visual: WPrice — the product card: ❓PRODUCT NAME, ❓PRICE; a real Checkout link
scenes.text: So here is the product. ❓PRODUCT, ❓PRICE. One real checkout link, live on the internet right now. And here is the rule: I don't pay myself and call it revenue. ❓WHO PAYS — stated plainly, on screen.

scenes.visual: WCheckout — SiteFrame: the Stripe Checkout page, card entry blurred in-plate, Pay button
scenes.text: Card in. Pay.

scenes.visual: WWebhookLog — Stripe dashboard webhook log → terminal: event received, signature ok, ledger row 1
scenes.text: Stripe fires the event. The service checks the signature. Checks the mode. Checks the product, the amount, the currency. Writes one row. Grants the access. Four seconds, end to end.

scenes.visual: WLands — the bottom-bar counter POPS $0.00 → $1.00 (or ❓PRICE); PAYOUT lights; chime
scenes.text: And there it is. The counter moves. Not a mockup. Not a staging key. Eleven episodes of zero — and one real dollar, from a real card, through a pipe you just watched get built. PAYOUT lights when the bank confirms — ❓ two business days. We'll show the statement next episode.

scenes.visual: WFails — the counter stays $0.00; the failing step flashes red; trap-snap
scenes.text: And — nothing. The counter doesn't move. ❓WHAT FAILED. That's the episode. I promised you'd watch it land or fail, and this is what failing looks like. Here's exactly where it broke, and here's what gets fixed before the next one.

scenes.visual: WHuman — 90/10 echo from ep10 and ep11
scenes.text: The fleet wrote the pipe. The fleet hardened it, audited it, and tonight deployed it. But look at what it could not do. It cannot open a Stripe account. It cannot sign the terms. It cannot put a legal name on the payout and carry the liability if something goes wrong. That ten percent is a human. That ten percent is why the ninety can be trusted with money at all.

scenes.visual: WOneDollar — checklist: pipe wired ✓, first dollar (✓ or ✗), second dollar from a stranger ☐
scenes.text: Full honesty, like always. One dollar is not a business. One dollar from a known card is a plumbing test. The real milestone is the second dollar — from a stranger, who found this company through the wheel, and paid because the product was worth it. That's the one that proves the flywheel.

scenes.visual: WNext — the promise card
scenes.text: Next episode: the stranger's dollar. Where they came from, which product, and what the wheel did to bring them. The counter stays on screen from here on. It doesn't reset.

scenes.visual: WOutro — Subscribe pill + link + BUILD./SHIP./REPEAT. landing word-by-word on his words
scenes.text: This was DansLab, number twelve. The First Dollar. If you want to see the second one land — subscribe, and hit like. You'll be here when it happens. Build. Ship. Repeat.
